body.text: Coffee manufacturers quietly change marketing after price squeeze
In short:
Major supermarket coffee brands have changed their marketing in response to bean prices surging to almost 50-year highs.
Some companies no longer label their products as "100 per cent arabica" but instead as "coffee", or mix the more expensive arabica beans with cheaper robusta beans.
What's next?
Experts and consumers want companies to flag recipe changes to buyers.
Major supermarket coffee brands have quietly changed their marketing in response to bean prices surging to almost 50-year highs.

Labelling of premium arabica coffee beans, prized for their sweeter, more complex flavour, has switched in some cases from "100 per cent arabica" to being described as "coffee", or as a blend with robusta, a more bitter variety of the plant.
While the change is legal and does not necessarily mean the coffee is worse, experts say consumers deserve to know when changes are made.
Cairns pensioner Brian Rantzau said price was his most important consideration when buying coffee, but he also wanted clear information about changes to the product.
"As a pensioner, you've got to mind every dollar," Mr Rantzau said.
"It should really tell us what's in it, right?"
The price of Mr Rantzau's preferred Coles's Organic Fairtrade Gold Freeze Dried Coffee has doubled since early 2024, jumping from $4 per 100 grams to $8.
Earlier this year, the product's "100 per cent arabica" description was also changed to simply read "instant coffee".
Both versions may appear on supermarket shelves at the same time as stores gradually phase out the old recipe.
Gold Coast mother Vicki Jarvis said she stopped buying the product.
"It just kept going up, and now it's $8 a jar, and I just would not pay that," she said.
"[But] if they've gone and changed what is actually in it, it should be written on the front of the label to let people know."
A Coles spokesperson said product formulations may need to change occasionally in response to ingredient availability and supply conditions.
"We work closely with our suppliers to ensure our products continue to meet our quality standards and provide great value for customers," the spokesperson said.
'Consumers should feel ripped off'
Australian food labelling rules do not require coffee companies to identify the species of bean unless they make a specific claim about it.
University of Queensland sensory scientist Heather Smyth said consumers had every right to feel ripped off.
Professor Smyth said consumers should be told when a product they had previously chosen for a key ingredient had changed.
"Consumers should feel ripped off if something very small has changed in a product and the makers of that product are not declaring what that change is,"
Jason Lilienstein runs a specialty roaster in Toowoomba, Queensland, and has only ever used arabica beans, bought directly from Colombian farmers he has met personally.
"Arabica has always been the preferred, high-quality bean," he said.
Robusta is not necessarily bad, he said, but he has not found one good enough for his blends.
"I haven't found it of sufficient quality to put in any of our coffee at this stage."
He said his customers tended to focus less on the species of bean and more on its flavour and origin.
Changing blends
Coffee prices have soared recently, with arabica prices reaching $15.40 a kilogram, while robusta hit $8.73 a kilogram — levels not seen since 1977 — piling pressure onto manufacturers.
While prices have fallen about 35 per cent from their peak ahead of what is expected to be a record Brazilian harvest, some say consumers may not see lower prices as other costs continue to rise.
Some coffee manufacturers have responded by adjusting the composition of their blends.

Australian-owned coffee manufacturer Vittoria's website once prominently promoted its coffee as "100 per cent arabica", stating in 2020: "At Vittoria coffee, we make no excuses, all our coffee is 100 per cent arabica".
And in mid-2025, the company's website described robusta as an "inferior quality bean".
But a few months later, that message had changed.
"If you're anti-robusta, try a freshly roasted blend that has been thoughtfully and scientifically created for consistency and flavour; you may be surprised at the result," the website said.
In a statement, managing director Rolando Schirato said the company had since removed "100 per cent arabica" branding from some products to give consumers a more affordable option.
He said whole bean and instant products remained predominantly arabica.
"We introduced a proportion of robusta into a small number of blends so that customers would have a more affordable option," he said.
Mr Schirato also said coffee companies routinely changed blends to maintain a consistent taste as crops, growing conditions and coffee availability changed.
"It is not practical to label these adjustments, particularly as packaging is produced well in advance of the coffee that goes into it,"
he said.
While the change is recent for some, the world's biggest food company, Nescafé, has used robusta in some of its premium Gold products in Australia for more than a decade.

"[We] have used carefully balanced blends of arabica and robusta to deliver the flavour, aroma and coffee experience consumers expect from each product. This remains unchanged," beverages general manager Martin Brown said in a statement.
Moccona, owned by JDE Peet's, has also removed "100 per cent arabica" wording from its instant coffee jars, replacing it with "100 per cent coffee beans".
JDE Peet's Australia marketing and transformation director Hilary Pulver said in 2019 that it updated the blends for Moccona Indulgence and Rich "to provide greater supply flexibility".
"This change helps ensure our ability to source quality beans from a range of coffee-growing regions, while keeping the taste of our products consistent," Ms Pulver said in a statement.
"The packaging was updated at the same time to reflect the change."
Professor Smyth said consumers of black coffee were most likely to notice the change in flavour if they did not spot the change in labelling.
"Anyone who's drinking a black coffee, a long black … those will be the consumers who are most impacted," she said.
